newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Strong Irish credit growth seen in July.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Strong Irish credit growth seen in July.

text.p: Irish credit growth, a cause of concern to the central bank in recent months, is expected to remain strong in July, analysts said on Tuesday.
Analysts' forecasts for underlying credit growth, due for release by the Central Bank at 1530 GMT on Thursday, range from 13.0 to 13.9 percent compared with 13.3 percent in June.

June's stronger-than-expected lending growth triggered a tightening of wholesale rates and a subsequent round of retail interest rate rises. Analysts say this month's data will be watched closely by the market.

"There is a degree of nervousness ahead of the figure particularly after the fallout from the last one so the short end of the market will certainly be very sensitive to it," said Dermot O'Brien, economist at NCB Stockbrokers.
O'Brien is among the few expecting a slight slowdown in credit growth to 13.0 percent in July.

"What seems likely is that the mortgage side of it will remain strong, even increase a little, but non-mortgage credit should slow and it was this which drove up the figures in the previous two months," he said.
But most other analysts expect credit growth to remain on an upward track.

Davy Stockbrokers expects a mild acceleration to 13.6 percent, Goodbody forecasts credit growth of 13.7 percent, Riada forecasts a 13.9 percent growth rate, and Bloxham expects a rate of 13.5 percent.
These growth rates are well above the central bank's single- digit target but views are mixed on the likely market impact of the data.
"The figures will be regarded as history," said Jim O'Leary, economist at Davy Stockbrokers.

"The last round of retail rate increases occurred on the back of central bank actions that presumably reflected central bank information about the state of play in July, how things were evolving in July," he told Reuters.
But others believe the figures will keep upward pressure on Irish wholesale rates.
"Such a rate of expanion will maintain the pressure on wholesale/retail interest rates in the near term," said Alan McQuaid of Bloxham.

McQuaid says credit will probably continue to grow in the short term, possibly leading to a 25-basis point rise in official Irish interest rates and another round of retail rate hikes before year-end.
Analysts say they will keep an eye on the end-July level of Irish official external reserves following rumours that the central bank intervened to support the Irish pound in July.
The reserves, which will be released with the credit data, are expected to fall by 100-200 million Irish pounds.
